items.title: Roland Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000
items.q: every time he couldn’t do it he’d call me and say, “Roland, would you take over for me?”

ctx.x: In 1970 — well tell me about your knighthood.

Oh that was a great experience for me. In 1969 I had been with the Thad Jones band for about two and a half, not quite three years, because Hank [Jones] started with him even though Thad and I talked about my being part of the band before he hired Hank, when he finally did it he hired Hank. But Hank was busy with television and couldn’t do it all the time so every time he couldn’t do it he’d call me and say, “Roland, would you take over for me?” Of course I took over. And finally sometime in ’66 I had a lot of…

began to hear me play and one night in my studio on 73rd Street in Manhattan, somebody called and asked me if I would consider coming to Liberia to play concerts. And of course I said yes immediately. There was no money involved. They had no money to pay. But they needed some people to play. And it turned out that they were asking people from various countries to contribute their part in the concert situation so they could raise money to build schools in Monrovia. And Jimmy Randolph or James Cheatham, I don’t…

items.title: Jones Hank — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I did a date like that and I think Roland Hanna was involved.

ctx.x: Talk about the four piano scenario.

I did a date like that and I think Roland Hanna was involved. Patty Bowen, Dick Hymen, and myself. Yes. I did a couple of those. One of them was with John Costa – – Eddie Costa, a pianist from Canada. I have done three of those things, you know? I don't remember who the third person was on the other one. None of them made that much noise anyway.
Were you pleased with them musically?
